title: Chapter X

teacherSummary.text: On the glacier Montanvert, the creature approaches. Victor curses it; the creature answers eloquently, reminding Victor of his duties: 'I ought to be thy Adam, but I am rather the fallen angel.' He asks Victor to hear his story, and Victor follows him to a hut.

vocabulary.definition: To make foul, impure, or unclean
vocabulary.context: We rise; one wand’ring thought pollutes the day.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “pollute”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: To feel sorrow, pain, or regret for
vocabulary.context: Listen to my tale: when you have heard that, abandon or commiserate me, as you shall judge that I deserve.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “commiserate”: com- (Latin com-, "with, together") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To infuse new life or spirit into
vocabulary.context: All of soul-inspiriting fled with sleep, and dark melancholy clouded every thought.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “inspirit”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Begone, vile insect! or rather, stay, that I may trample you to dust! and, oh! that I could, with the extinction of your miserable existence, restore those victims whom you have so diabolically murdered!”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “diabolical”: -al (Latin -alis, "relating to"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To look down upon from a place that is over or above
vocabulary.context: For some time I sat upon the rock that overlooks the sea of ice.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “overlook”: over- (Old English ofer, "over"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Remember, that I am thy creature; I ought to be thy Adam; but I am rather the fallen angel, whom thou drivest from joy for no misdeed.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “misdeed”: mis- (Old English mis-, "wrongly"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To call upon, or for, in supplication
vocabulary.context: Will no entreaties cause thee to turn a favourable eye upon thy creature, who implores thy goodness and compassion?
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “implore”: im- (Latin in-, "not" or "in") + plor (Latin plorare, "to wail"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: The sun is yet high in the heavens; before it descends to hide itself behind yon snowy precipices, and illuminate another world, you will have heard my story, and can decide.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “illuminate”: il- (Latin in-, "not") + lum (Latin lumen, "light") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: I stood beside the sources of the Arveiron, which take their rise in a glacier, that with slow pace is advancing down from the summit of the hills, to barricade the valley.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “barricade”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: To scatter or set here and there among other things
vocabulary.context: The surface is very uneven, rising like the waves of a troubled sea, descending low, and interspersed by rifts that sink deep.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “intersperse”: inter- (Latin inter, "between"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Milton's Paradise Lost shapes the creature's self-understanding—God and Adam, Satan the outcast.

significance: The creature's eloquence overturns expectations of a mindless monster and shifts our sympathies.
discussionQuestions: The creature says, 'I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend.' Do you believe him?
Where does allusion appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with the costs of unchecked ambition?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter X,” how does Shelley show confrontation between creator and creation? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the allusion you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter X develops the idea of confrontation between creator and creation. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of allusion and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Mary Shelley uses allusion in Chapter X to complicate the reader's understanding of confrontation between creator and creation. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter X within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of confrontation between creator and creation responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter X as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of confrontation between creator and creation. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Frankenstein.

satQuestions.passage:
We rest; a dream has power to poison sleep.
We rise; one wand’ring thought pollutes the day.
We feel, conceive, or reason; laugh or weep,
Embrace fond woe, or cast our cares away;
It is the same: for, be it joy or sorrow,
The path of its departure still is free.
Man’s yesterday may ne’er be like his morrow;
Nought may endure but mutability!
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter X”?

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: The creature says, 'I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend.' Do you believe him? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are pollutes, commiserate, inspiriting, diabolically, overlooks. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “We rise; one wand’ring thought pollutes the day.” Webster's says: To make foul, impure, or unclean. Now the word history: “pollute”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “commiserate”: com- (Latin com-, "with, together") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “inspirit”: in- (Latin in-, "not" or "in"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Frankenstein would have known. Milton's Paradise Lost shapes the creature's self-understanding—God and Adam, Satan the outcast. Why does this chapter matter? The creature's eloquence overturns expectations of a mindless monster and shifts our sympathies. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for allusion.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see allusion, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to confrontation between creator and creation.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Allusion, Characterization, Irony.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of allusion. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Allusion, Characterization, Irony: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter X,” how does Shelley show confrontation between creator and creation? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the allusion you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the costs of unchecked ambition? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about confrontation between creator and creation, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how allusion shapes confrontation between creator and creation. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
